text: What is the best translation of the Bible into English available today? Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlullen. I'm a scholar of the Bible and religion and I
get this question every single day. And to kind of give away the store a little bit, the updated edition of the New Revised Standard Version is usually the
translation that I recommend. However, I usually start off by saying it depends.
It depends on why you're engaging the text, how you want it to function. Do you want it to have a literary function?
Do you want it to have a missionary function, an administrative function, an apologetic function? And what are you bringing to the table? Do you have
degrees in English literature, or is English a second language for you? Are you looking for a translation for a 12-year-old? There are a lot of
different reasons people engage the Bible. And so, a lot of different dimensions of quality that can intersect. And usually when I tell
people this, they say, "I just want to try to get the closest to what the authors originally meant." So there's a degree of originalism that is being
prioritized. Most of the time I'm asked this question. And so in determining which one is best, I consider three main
dimensions of quality. One is the scholarship. What kinds of manuscripts are the translators relying on? What kinds of text critical decisions are
they relying on? what kinds of theological dogmas and frameworks are going into how they're rendering the
text. Another is the translation technique. Translation is really a balancing act. How much work is the translator willing to put in to bring
the text closer to the target audience so that they have to do less work. And on the other side of that, we have translations that demand a lot of work
from the target audience. They have to have an awful lot of understanding of the source culture in order to be able to get the most out of the translation.
But that translation is therefore going to be closest to the source text. And so it's a balancing act between
accessibility and faithfulness. So that's another dimension of quality. And that's usually going to be related to the third dimension of quality, which is the language register that's being used.
How accessible is it to a reader of English? Is it accessible to somebody who understands English as a second language, or are they going to need to
know an awful lot of the intricacies of how English works literally,
rhetorically, and all of that kind of stuff? But when we consider all of those things and you're looking for a Bible that contains the Hebrew Bible and the
New Testament together, I usually recommend the updated edition of the New Revised Standard Version. And the edition that I usually recommend right
now is the SBL study bible which just came out a couple years ago because it has the entire NRSVUE including the
Apocrypha or the Duderro canonical books. It has wonderful explanatory notes. It has wonderful introductions to the books as well as little mini essays
in sidebars that explain things here and there that usually you're not going to find in a translation. And then there's another uh study Bible, the Westminster
study Bible that also incorporates the updated edition of the New Revised Standard Version that also just came out that also has wonderful introductions,
wonderful explanatory notes, and even essays and things like that. Now, before the NRSV UEIE came out a few years ago,
I would recommend the fifth edition of the New Oxford Annotated Bible, and the sixth edition will be coming out in the next year or two, and that will
incorporate the updated edition of the New Revised Standard Version, and I will probably shift my allegiances to that translation once it comes out, but we'll
have to see how it goes. Now, there are other translations out there that are also very good uh in their own ways. The
NASB does some good things. The NIV does some good things when it comes to uh accessibility, but it also presupposes
univocality and inspiration, which means it's fiddling with the language and the translation in order to make it seem like it agrees in places where it
actually disagrees. The ESV does some very good things, I think, but it is fundamentally a complimentarian Bible
translation. It is intended to defend the subordination of women to men. And so a lot of its translation choices are
deeply problematic. And I don't recommend the ESV and particularly not study editions of the ESV. If you're
just looking for a Hebrew Bible, Robert Alter recently published his own translation of the Hebrew Bible that is very, very good and has a lot of
explanatory notes. It's more of a literary project and so a lot of the notes are going to discuss literary
concerns as well as some theological concerns but not so much text critical concerns and historical concerns and
things like that. There's also the JPS Tanakh which is the translation of the Jewish Publication Society. This is a Jewish translation. It is very good. The
second edition of the Jewish Study Bible incorporates this translation and also has wonderful explanatory notes and things like that. There is also the very
thorough JPS Torah commentary series if you would like commentary from phenomenal scholars on the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, the books of
Moses. And there's also a wonderful Jewish annotated New Testament that uses the NRSV, but the explanatory notes, the
introductions, the commentary come from Jewish scholars who are situating the New Testament within a Jewish context to
explain how these things relate to what was going on within Judaism at the time.
Now, if you're looking for just a New Testament on its own, I still think the NRSVUEE does the best job of those that
are available. Obviously, I don't agree with all of it. There are aspects of it that I criticize, but I think it's better than the other translations that
are coming out. People will ask about David Bentley Hart's translation of the New Testament. That's an interesting project. I think it's a little
idiosyncratic. I would love to have more explanatory notes. One of the main ideas was to render the English in a way that
simulates the experience of the Greek reader. So if it's very sophisticated Greek, the English is going to be sophisticated. If it's very awkward Greek, the English is going to be very
awkward. So it's a little idiosyncratic in that regard. Sarah Ruden has published her own translation of the Gospels that is very good. This uses
transliteration for place names and personal names and things like that.
it's going to be a little more sophisticated. So maybe a little less accessible for someone who does not have a strong grasp of the English language.
And so in striking that balance between accessibility and faithfulness, I'm probably going to say the NRSVE even for the New Testament. So
those are the translations that I think do the best. Overall, the one that I think scores the highest when I consider all the different dimensions of quality
and consider what people are coming to me asking about, I would say the updated edition of the NRSVE is the best
available translation. And the fit for this video has been Hasbin Hotel.
